evidence.title: Application of Generalized Composite Multiscale Lempel-Ziv Complexity in Identifying Wind Turbine Gearbox Faults.
evidence.abstract: Wind turbine gearboxes operate in harsh environments; therefore, the resulting gear vibration signal has characteristics of strong nonlinearity, is non-stationary, and has a low signal-to-noise ratio, which indicates that it is difficult to identify wind turbine gearbox faults effectively by the traditional methods. To solve this problem, this paper proposes a new fault diagnosis method for wind turbine gearboxes based on generalized composite multiscale Lempel-Ziv complexity (GCMLZC). Within the proposed method, an effective technique named multiscale morphological-hat convolution operator (MHCO) is firstly presented to remove the noise interference information of the original gear vibration signal. Then, the GCMLZC of the filtered signal was calculated to extract gear fault features. Finally, the extracted fault features were input into softmax classifier for automatically identifying different health conditions of wind turbine gearboxes. The effectiveness of the proposed method was validated by the experimental and engineering data analysis. The results of the analysis indicate that the proposed method can identify accurately different gear health conditions. Moreover, the identification accuracy of the proposed method is higher than that of traditional multiscale Lempel-Ziv complexity (MLZC) and several representative multiscale entropies (e.g., multiscale dispersion entropy (MDE), multiscale permutation entropy (MPE) and multiscale sample entropy (MSE)).

evidence.title: Predictive maintenance of planetary gearboxes using FFT and machine learning technique
evidence.abstract: Planetary gearboxes are widely used in manufacturing processes, and non-destructive assessment is becoming increasingly important for monitoring their state. We outlined a fine-tuned random decision tree (FT-RDT) in this study for classifying and fault-finding the gearbox via signals generated by vibrations. This approach concentrates on the identification of worn gears, consequently distinct classes—healthy gears, ringed gears containing damaged tooth faces, and planetary gears featuring damaged tooth faces—were established. Each of the categories consists of 150 specimens, divided into two separate sets of 50 specimens for the testing data and 100 specimens for the data used for training. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) was used to convert the temporal signals to frequencies. The next step was to gather 24 statistical characteristics from frequency data. The retrieved characteristic was fed into the fault classification procedure (FT-RDT). Combining these methods yields rates of classification accuracy across train and test data of 92.75% and 91.50%, demonstrating the excellent reliability and capability of the problem identification solution that is created.

evidence.abstract: Farm machinery significantly enhances agricultural productivity but remains a leading source of occupational injuries, particularly in resource-limited settings. This comprehensive review synthesises the primary human-, equipment-, environmental-, and weather-related causes of such injuries and critically evaluates mitigation strategies, incorporating new evidence on the interplay between machinery reliability and operator safety. A systematic review integrated literature published 2000-2025 across multiple databases. Intervention effectiveness was appraised using a multi-step methodology combining GRADE-based quality assessment, statistical inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ  =  0.84), and internal reliability testing (Cronbach's α  =  0.83). The findings reveal that human factors, including inadequate training, fatigue, and cognitive decline, are the most prevalent risk contributors, followed by equipment-related issues such as outdated machinery and poor maintenance, and context-specific environmental and weather hazards. High-impact interventions include mandatory operator training, preventive and predictive maintenance protocols, retrofitting safety-critical components, and deploying sensor-based hazard detection. The newly integrated reliability framework highlights four mutually reinforcing pillars-design, maintenance, operations, and management systems-that demonstrate how engineering reliability directly reduces hazardous failures and improves safety metrics. This evidence-driven synthesis underscores the need to combine human factors interventions, ergonomic design, environmental adaptations, weather preparedness, and engineering reliability improvements to achieve the strongest safety outcomes, especially when supported by policy enforcement and training systems.

Intervention effectiveness was appraised using a multi-step methodology combining GRADE-based quality assessment, statistical inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ  =  0.84), and internal reliability testing (Cronbach's α  =  0.83). The findings reveal that human factors, including inadequate training, fatigue, and cognitive decline, are the most prevalent risk contributors, followed by equipment-related issues such as outdated machinery and poor maintenance, and context-specific environmental and weather hazards. High-impact interventions include mandatory operator training, preventive and predictive maintenance protocols, retrofitting safety-critical components, and deploying sensor-based hazard detection. The newly integrated reliability framework highlights four mutually reinforcing pillars-design, maintenance, operations, and management systems-that demonstrate how engineering reliability directly reduces hazardous failures and improves safety metrics. This evidence-driven synthesis underscores the need to combine human factors interventions, ergonomic design, environmental adaptations, weather preparedness, and engineering reliability improvements to achieve the strongest safety outcomes, especially when supported by policy enforcement and training systems.

items.record_text: Predictive maintenance of planetary gearboxes using FFT and machine learning technique Planetary gearboxes are widely used in manufacturing processes, and non-destructive assessment is becoming increasingly important for monitoring their state. We outlined a fine-tuned random decision tree (FT-RDT) in this study for classifying and fault-finding the gearbox via signals generated by vibrations. This approach concentrates on the identification of worn gears, consequently distinct classes—healthy gears, ringed gears containing damaged tooth faces, and planetary gears featuring damaged tooth faces—were established. Each of the categories consists of 150 specimens, divided into two separate sets of 50 specimens for the testing data and 100 specimens for the data used for training. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) was used to convert the temporal signals to frequencies. The next step was to gather 24 statistical characteristics from frequency data. The retrieved characteristic was fed into the fault classification procedure (FT-RDT). Combining these methods yields rates of classification accuracy across train and test data of 92.75% and 91.50%, demonstrating the excellent reliability and capability of the problem identification solution that is created.

warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

custody_records.raw_content: Wind turbine gearboxes operate in harsh environments; therefore, the resulting gear vibration signal has characteristics of strong nonlinearity, is non-stationary, and has a low signal-to-noise ratio, which indicates that it is difficult to identify wind turbine gearbox faults effectively by the traditional methods. To solve this problem, this paper proposes a new fault diagnosis method for wind turbine gearboxes based on generalized composite multiscale Lempel-Ziv complexity (GCMLZC). Within the proposed method, an effective technique named multiscale morphological-hat convolution operator (MHCO) is firstly presented to remove the noise interference information of the original gear vibration signal. Then, the GCMLZC of the filtered signal was calculated to extract gear fault features. Finally, the extracted fault features were input into softmax classifier for automatically identifying different health conditions of wind turbine gearboxes. The effectiveness of the proposed method was validated by the experimental and engineering data analysis. The results of the analysis indicate that the proposed method can identify accurately different gear health conditions. Moreover, the identification accuracy of the proposed method is higher than that of traditional multiscale Lempel-Ziv complexity (MLZC) and several representative multiscale entropies (e.g., multiscale dispersion entropy (MDE), multiscale permutation entropy (MPE) and multiscale sample entropy (MSE)).

custody_records.raw_content: Planetary gearboxes are widely used in manufacturing processes, and non-destructive assessment is becoming increasingly important for monitoring their state. We outlined a fine-tuned random decision tree (FT-RDT) in this study for classifying and fault-finding the gearbox via signals generated by vibrations. This approach concentrates on the identification of worn gears, consequently distinct classes—healthy gears, ringed gears containing damaged tooth faces, and planetary gears featuring damaged tooth faces—were established. Each of the categories consists of 150 specimens, divided into two separate sets of 50 specimens for the testing data and 100 specimens for the data used for training. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) was used to convert the temporal signals to frequencies. The next step was to gather 24 statistical characteristics from frequency data. The retrieved characteristic was fed into the fault classification procedure (FT-RDT). Combining these methods yields rates of classification accuracy across train and test data of 92.75% and 91.50%, demonstrating the excellent reliability and capability of the problem identification solution that is created.

custody_records.raw_content: Farm machinery significantly enhances agricultural productivity but remains a leading source of occupational injuries, particularly in resource-limited settings. This comprehensive review synthesises the primary human-, equipment-, environmental-, and weather-related causes of such injuries and critically evaluates mitigation strategies, incorporating new evidence on the interplay between machinery reliability and operator safety. A systematic review integrated literature published 2000-2025 across multiple databases. Intervention effectiveness was appraised using a multi-step methodology combining GRADE-based quality assessment, statistical inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ  =  0.84), and internal reliability testing (Cronbach's α  =  0.83). The findings reveal that human factors, including inadequate training, fatigue, and cognitive decline, are the most prevalent risk contributors, followed by equipment-related issues such as outdated machinery and poor maintenance, and context-specific environmental and weather hazards. High-impact interventions include mandatory operator training, preventive and predictive maintenance protocols, retrofitting safety-critical components, and deploying sensor-based hazard detection. The newly integrated reliability framework highlights four mutually reinforcing pillars-design, maintenance, operations, and management systems-that demonstrate how engineering reliability directly reduces hazardous failures and improves safety metrics. This evidence-driven synthesis underscores the need to combine human factors interventions, ergonomic design, environmental adaptations, weather preparedness, and engineering reliability improvements to achieve the strongest safety outcomes, especially when supported by policy enforcement and training systems.

These systems operate under challenging enviromental conditions and failure of some of their parts, for the time being, is frequent, although undesirable. Wind turbine gearboxes, more particularly, seem to be so problematic that some wind turbine designs avoid including them. Structural health monitoring and condition monitoring of wind turbines appear to be necessary in order to determine the condition and lifespan of the wind turbine components and the drivetrain respectively. In this way reparative actions could be taken whenever needed resulting in reduction of maintenance costs.

This shows a demand for effective methods for early damage detection. Developments in the area of advanced signal processing should be examined and applied in damage detection of wind turbine gearboxes.
